\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }18\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(10).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+81Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+81\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+81\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{18}\pi E\left(\frac{80}{81}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
18 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{80}{81}\right)

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The defining series solves }z^2J_n\prime\prime+zJ_n\prime+(z^2-n^2)J_n=0.\textnormal{Differentiate the expression }F(z)=\frac{z^2}{2}J_n\prime(z)^2+\frac{z^2-n^2}{2}J_n(z)^2.\textnormal{The equation gives }F\prime(z)=zJ_n(z)^2.
\textnormal{The series shows the lower endpoint contribution is zero. At the chosen root, }F(\alpha)=\frac{\alpha^2}{2}J_{0}\prime(\alpha)^2.

\textnormal{The series also gives the recurrence }J_n\prime(z)=\frac nzJ_n(z)-J_{n+1}(z).\textnormal{At the root, use this relation and then substitute }z=\alpha r\textnormal{ in the requested integral.}
\frac{J^{2}_{1}\left(\alpha\right)}{2}
sourceCanonical.statement: J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}\quad(n=0,1,2,\ldots).\textnormal{Let alpha be the }1\textnormal{-th positive zero of }J_{0}.\textnormal{Evaluate }\int_0^1r\,J_{0}(\alpha r)^2\,\mathrm dr.

analyticCertificate: Termwise differentiation of the entire series gives the Bessel ODE, its derivative recurrence, and the regular-origin behavior. For order zero the derivative is O(z), and for positive integer order the function is O(z^n); these imply F(0)=0. A positive root and its derivative cannot both vanish by uniqueness for the nonsingular ODE at that point. Existence and ordering of positive Bessel zeros are standard oscillation-theory prerequisites, not asserted as machine proved. All positive zeros exceed two: on (0,2], the defining alternating series has decreasing term magnitudes; for positive integer order its first term strictly exceeds the second, and for order zero at z=2 the first two cancel but the remaining alternating tail is strictly positive. Thus alpha squared exceeds four. Together with the nonzero root derivative, this strictly orders all authored alternatives and certifies their inequivalence; symbolic non-simplification alone is not used as that proof.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,100),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }20\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(11).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+100Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+100\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+100\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{20}\pi E\left(\frac{99}{100}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
20 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{99}{100}\right)
sourceCanonical.statement: \textnormal{Let }A,B,C,D\textnormal{ be independent real standard-normal random variables, each with density }(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}.\textnormal{Let }\mathcal L\textnormal{ be the total Euclidean curve length of the zero set in the displayed square; counting or omitting the boundary does not affect this length almost surely. Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(10y)+D\sin(10y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The defining series solves }z^2J_n\prime\prime+zJ_n\prime+(z^2-n^2)J_n=0.\textnormal{Differentiate the expression }F(z)=\frac{z^2}{2}J_n\prime(z)^2+\frac{z^2-n^2}{2}J_n(z)^2.\textnormal{The equation gives }F\prime(z)=zJ_n(z)^2.
\textnormal{The series shows the lower endpoint contribution is zero. At the chosen root, }F(\alpha)=\frac{\alpha^2}{2}J_{4}\prime(\alpha)^2.

\textnormal{The series also gives the recurrence }J_n\prime(z)=\frac nzJ_n(z)-J_{n+1}(z).\textnormal{At the root, use this relation and then substitute }z=\alpha r\textnormal{ in the requested integral.}
\frac{J^{2}_{5}\left(\alpha\right)}{2}
sourceCanonical.statement: J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}\quad(n=0,1,2,\ldots).\textnormal{Let alpha be the }1\textnormal{-th positive zero of }J_{4}.\textnormal{Evaluate }\int_0^1r\,J_{4}(\alpha r)^2\,\mathrm dr.

analyticCertificate: Termwise differentiation of the entire series gives the Bessel ODE, its derivative recurrence, and the regular-origin behavior. For order zero the derivative is O(z), and for positive integer order the function is O(z^n); these imply F(0)=0. A positive root and its derivative cannot both vanish by uniqueness for the nonsingular ODE at that point. Existence and ordering of positive Bessel zeros are standard oscillation-theory prerequisites, not asserted as machine proved. All positive zeros exceed two: on (0,2], the defining alternating series has decreasing term magnitudes; for positive integer order its first term strictly exceeds the second, and for order zero at z=2 the first two cancel but the remaining alternating tail is strictly positive. Thus alpha squared exceeds four. Together with the nonzero root derivative, this strictly orders all authored alternatives and certifies their inequivalence; symbolic non-simplification alone is not used as that proof.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,36),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }12\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(7).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+36Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+36\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+36\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{12}\pi E\left(\frac{35}{36}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}

Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(6y)+D\sin(6y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

\textnormal{Set }s=t\textnormal{, integrate, and use symmetry: the requested squared norm is }-\frac{T\prime(a)}{2a}\textnormal{ evaluated at }5.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{25},\frac{26}{25}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{25}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{25}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{25}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{5},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}

The inverse hyperbolic sine has its real convention }\operatorname{arcsinh}v=\ln(v+\sqrt{1+v^2}).

analyticCertificate: Termwise differentiation of the entire series gives the Bessel ODE, its derivative recurrence, and the regular-origin behavior. For order zero the derivative is O(z), and for positive integer order the function is O(z^n); these imply F(0)=0. A positive root and its derivative cannot both vanish by uniqueness for the nonsingular ODE at that point. Existence and ordering of positive Bessel zeros are standard oscillation-theory prerequisites, not asserted as machine proved. All positive zeros exceed two: on (0,2], the defining alternating series has decreasing term magnitudes; for positive integer order its first term strictly exceeds the second, and for order zero at z=2 the first two cancel but the remaining alternating tail is strictly positive. Thus alpha squared exceeds four. Together with the nonzero root derivative, this strictly orders all authored alternatives and certifies their inequivalence; symbolic non-simplification alone is not used as that proof.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{1}(1-u^2)^{1}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{12}{5}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\sin t\,\mathrm dt=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi}{\cosh(\pi/2)},\qquad M_A(\phi)=-\frac{12}{5}+\frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}A\sin\phi.
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
\frac{6 \sqrt{2} \cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}{5 \pi}
sourceCanonical.statement: x\prime\prime=x-x^3+\varepsilon\left[-(1+x^{2})x\prime+A\cos t\right],\qquad A>0.\textnormal{Let }x_h\textnormal{ be the positive unperturbed homoclinic orbit with its maximum at zero, and put }v_h=x_h\prime.\textnormal{Define the first-order Melnikov function by }M_A(\phi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\left[-(1+x_h(t)^{2})v_h(t)+A\cos(t+\phi)\right]\,\mathrm dt.\textnormal{Find }\inf\{A>0:M_A\textnormal{ has a simple real zero}\}.

analyticCertificate: The orbit decays exponentially, so all work and Fourier integrals converge absolutely. The Fourier beta integral has complex parameter (1+i)/2 with real part one half; Euler reflection gives pi/cosh(pi/2). Integration by parts has vanishing boundary terms. The sine function has simple intersections with a horizontal level strictly between minus one and one; equality gives a double tangency. This proves the infimum directly from the definition without invoking any finite-epsilon dynamical conclusion.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{2}(1-u^2)^{2}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{268}{105}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\sin t\,\mathrm dt=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi}{\cosh(\pi/2)},\qquad M_A(\phi)=-\frac{268}{105}+\frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}A\sin\phi.
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
\frac{134 \sqrt{2} \cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}{105 \pi}

analyticCertificate: The orbit decays exponentially, so all work and Fourier integrals converge absolutely. The Fourier beta integral has complex parameter (1+i)/2 with real part one half; Euler reflection gives pi/cosh(pi/2). Integration by parts has vanishing boundary terms. The sine function has simple intersections with a horizontal level strictly between minus one and one; equality gives a double tangency. This proves the infimum directly from the definition without invoking any finite-epsilon dynamical conclusion.

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }22\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(12).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+121Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+121\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+121\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{22}\pi E\left(\frac{120}{121}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}

The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(11y)+D\sin(11y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{6}(1-u^2)^{6}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{322204}{45045}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\sin t\,\mathrm dt=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi}{\cosh(\pi/2)},\qquad M_A(\phi)=-\frac{322204}{45045}+\frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}A\sin\phi.
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
\frac{161102 \sqrt{2} \cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}{45045 \pi}
sourceCanonical.statement: x\prime\prime=x-x^3+\varepsilon\left[-(1+x^{12})x\prime+A\cos t\right],\qquad A>0.\textnormal{Let }x_h\textnormal{ be the positive unperturbed homoclinic orbit with its maximum at zero, and put }v_h=x_h\prime.\textnormal{Define the first-order Melnikov function by }M_A(\phi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\left[-(1+x_h(t)^{12})v_h(t)+A\cos(t+\phi)\right]\,\mathrm dt.\textnormal{Find }\inf\{A>0:M_A\textnormal{ has a simple real zero}\}.

analyticCertificate: The orbit decays exponentially, so all work and Fourier integrals converge absolutely. The Fourier beta integral has complex parameter (1+i)/2 with real part one half; Euler reflection gives pi/cosh(pi/2). Integration by parts has vanishing boundary terms. The sine function has simple intersections with a horizontal level strictly between minus one and one; equality gives a double tangency. This proves the infimum directly from the definition without invoking any finite-epsilon dynamical conclusion.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,64),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }16\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(9).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+64Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+64\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+64\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{16}\pi E\left(\frac{63}{64}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
16 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{63}{64}\right)

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.

\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,49),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }14\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(8).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+49Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+49\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+49\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{14}\pi E\left(\frac{48}{49}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
14 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{48}{49}\right)

Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(7y)+D\sin(7y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{81},\frac{82}{81}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{81}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{9},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{16},\frac{17}{16}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{16}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{4},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{16},\frac{17}{16}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{16}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{4},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{With outward unit normal equal to the position vector on the unit sphere, Stokes gives }\iint_S\mathbf n\,\mathrm dS=\frac12\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf r\times\mathrm d\mathbf r.
\textnormal{A positively oriented shorter great-circle arc from U to V contributes }\arccos(U\cdot V)\,\frac{U\times V}{|U\times V|}.\textnormal{Use the boundary order A, B, C, A.}

\textnormal{The third components of the three unit edge normals are }1,\quad -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\quad -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\textnormal{and the corresponding arc lengths are }\frac{\pi}{2},\ \arccos{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \right)},\ \arccos{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \right)}.
- \frac{\sqrt{2} \arccos{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \right)}}{2} + \frac{\pi}{4}
sourceCanonical.statement: \textnormal{On the unit sphere, let S be the smaller spherical triangle in the positive octant bounded by the shorter great-circle arcs joining }A=(1,0,0),\quad B=(0,1,0),\quad C=\frac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt{3}}.\textnormal{Find }\iint_S z\,\mathrm dS.

analyticCertificate: For each constant vector e, the curl of (e cross r)/2 equals e, proving the vector Stokes identity. Parametrize a unit-speed great-circle arc as U cos(s)+V_perp sin(s); its cross product with its derivative is the constant oriented unit edge normal. The determinant of A,B,C is positive, giving the stated outward boundary order. The third component of the resulting vector is precisely the requested surface integral.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{10}(1-u^2)^{10}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{367829180}{7436429}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\sin t\,\mathrm dt=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi}{\cosh(\pi/2)},\qquad M_A(\phi)=-\frac{367829180}{7436429}+\frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}A\sin\phi.
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
\frac{183914590 \sqrt{2} \cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}{7436429 \pi}

analyticCertificate: Termwise differentiation of the entire series gives the Bessel ODE, its derivative recurrence, and the regular-origin behavior. A positive root and its derivative cannot both vanish by uniqueness for the nonsingular ODE at that point. Existence and ordering of positive Bessel zeros are standard oscillation-theory prerequisites, not asserted as machine proved. All positive zeros exceed two: on (0,2], the defining alternating series has decreasing term magnitudes; for positive integer order its first term strictly exceeds the second, and for order zero at z=2 the first two cancel but the remaining alternating tail is strictly positive. Thus alpha squared exceeds four. \textnormal{Use the angle appearing in the cross term to define a whitening transformation.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{64},\frac{65}{64}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{64}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{64}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{64}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{8},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,16),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }8\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(5).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+16Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+16\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+16\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{8}\pi E\left(\frac{15}{16}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
8 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{15}{16}\right)
sourceCanonical.statement: \textnormal{Let }A,B,C,D\textnormal{ be independent real standard-normal random variables, each with density }(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}.\textnormal{Let }\mathcal L\textnormal{ be the total Euclidean curve length of the zero set in the displayed square; counting or omitting the boundary does not affect this length almost surely. Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(4y)+D\sin(4y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Matching homogeneous solutions and the unit derivative jump gives the symmetric kernel }G_a(t,s)=\frac{\sinh(a\min\{t,s\})\sinh(a(1-\max\{t,s\}))}{a\sinh a}.
\textnormal{Its diagonal integral is }T(a)=\int_0^1G_a(t,t)\,\mathrm dt=\frac{\coth a}{2a}-\frac1{2a^2}.
\textnormal{Differentiate the defining operator equation in a. The same zero-boundary Green inverse gives }\partial_aG_a(t,s)=-2a\int_0^1G_a(t,r)G_a(r,s)\,\mathrm dr.
\textnormal{Set }s=t\textnormal{, integrate, and use symmetry: the requested squared norm is }-\frac{T\prime(a)}{2a}\textnormal{ evaluated at }4.
- \frac{1}{512} + \frac{1}{64 \sinh^{2}{\left(4 \right)}} + \frac{\coth{\left(4 \right)}}{256}
sourceCanonical.statement: \textnormal{For each }s\in(0,1),\textnormal{ let }G(t,s)\textnormal{ be continuous in }t\textnormal{, vanish at }t=0,1,\textnormal{ and satisfy }-G_{tt}+16G=0\quad(t\ne s),\quad G_t(s^+,s)-G_t(s^-,s)=-1.\textnormal{Evaluate }\int_0^1\int_0^1G(t,s)^2\,\mathrm dt\,\mathrm ds.

analyticCertificate: The homogeneous Dirichlet problem has only the zero solution, by integrating the positive energy, so the matched Green kernel is unique. Its compact-domain hyperbolic formula is smoothly parameter-dependent for positive a. Differentiating the inverse equation produces a source -2aG with zero boundaries; applying the same Green inverse proves the displayed resolvent identity. All compact integrals are continuous, so differentiation and integration commute.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,25),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }10\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(6).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+25Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+25\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+25\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{10}\pi E\left(\frac{24}{25}\right).
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
10 \sqrt{2} \pi E\left(\frac{24}{25}\right)

Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(5y)+D\sin(5y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{9},\frac{10}{9}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{9}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{3},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}
- \frac{19 \sqrt{10}}{54} + \frac{\operatorname{arcsinh}{\left(3 \right)}}{162} + \frac{10}{9}

Among all joint distributions with these two marginals, find the smallest expected squared Euclidean distance.}\quad \frac{1}{9}\le |Y|^2\le\frac{10}{9},\qquad\inf\mathbb E\bigl[|X-Y|^2\bigr]=?\textnormal{Here uniform means normalized planar area; dependence between X and Y may be chosen freely. The inverse hyperbolic sine has its real convention }\operatorname{arcsinh}v=\ln(v+\sqrt{1+v^2}).

Nonnegative layer-cake integration follows from Tonelli, and the intersection of two upper-tail intervals in a common uniform variable has probability equal to the smaller tail probability, establishing sharpness of the rearrangement bound. \textnormal{The series shows the lower endpoint contribution is zero. At the chosen root, }F(\alpha)=\frac{\alpha^2}{2}J_{3}\prime(\alpha)^2.

\textnormal{The series also gives the recurrence }J_n\prime(z)=\frac nzJ_n(z)-J_{n+1}(z).\textnormal{At the root, use this relation and then substitute }z=\alpha r\textnormal{ in the requested integral.}

analyticCertificate: Termwise differentiation of the entire series gives the Bessel ODE, its derivative recurrence, and the regular-origin behavior. For order zero the derivative is O(z), and for positive integer order the function is O(z^n); these imply F(0)=0. A positive root and its derivative cannot both vanish by uniqueness for the nonsingular ODE at that point. Existence and ordering of positive Bessel zeros are standard oscillation-theory prerequisites, not asserted as machine proved. All positive zeros exceed two: on (0,2], the defining alternating series has decreasing term magnitudes; for positive integer order its first term strictly exceeds the second, and for order zero at z=2 the first two cancel but the remaining alternating tail is strictly positive. Thus alpha squared exceeds four. Together with the nonzero root derivative, this strictly orders all authored alternatives and certifies their inequivalence; symbolic non-simplification alone is not used as that proof.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write R and S for the radii of X and Y. Their squared radii have uniform distributions on the respective area-coordinate intervals.}
R^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad S^2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[\frac{1}{49},\frac{50}{49}],\qquad\mathbb E|X-Y|^2=1+\frac{1}{49}-2\mathbb E(X\cdot Y).

\textnormal{Pointwise angular alignment gives X dot Y at most R times S. To maximize the product expectation of two nonnegative bounded variables, write it as the double integral of their joint survival probability. Each joint survival probability is at most the smaller marginal survival probability.}
\mathbb E(RS)=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv,\qquad\mathbb P(R>u,S>v)\le\min\{\mathbb P(R>u),\mathbb P(S>v)\}.

\textnormal{All these bounds are attained simultaneously by using the same uniform variable for both squared radii and the same independent uniform angle. This proves global optimality over all joint distributions.}
R=\sqrt U,\quad S=\sqrt{\frac{1}{49}+U},\quad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\qquad\max\mathbb E(X\cdot Y)=2\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{49}+r^2}\,\mathrm dr.

\textnormal{Let a denote the positive inner radius in this problem. A chosen primitive for the final one-variable integral is }a=\frac{1}{7},\qquad F(r)=\frac{r\sqrt{a^2+r^2}(a^2+2r^2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(r/a)}8.
\int_0^1r^2\sqrt{a^2+r^2}\,\mathrm dr=F(1)-F(0)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}(a^2+2)-a^4\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/a)}8.
\textnormal{Substitute this cross moment into the squared-distance identity.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{4}(1-u^2)^{4}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{12812}{3465}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\sin t\,\mathrm dt=-\frac{\sqrt2\pi}{\cosh(\pi/2)},\qquad M_A(\phi)=-\frac{12812}{3465}+\frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{\cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}A\sin\phi.
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
\frac{6406 \sqrt{2} \cosh{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}}{3465 \pi}

The Fourier beta integral has complex parameter (1+i)/2 with real part one half; Euler reflection gives pi/cosh(pi/2). Integration by parts has vanishing boundary terms. The sine function has simple intersections with a horizontal level strictly between minus one and one; equality gives a double tangency. This proves the infimum directly from the definition without invoking any finite-epsilon dynamical conclusion.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Matching homogeneous solutions and the unit derivative jump gives the symmetric kernel }G_a(t,s)=\frac{\sinh(a\min\{t,s\})\sinh(a(1-\max\{t,s\}))}{a\sinh a}.
\textnormal{Its diagonal integral is }T(a)=\int_0^1G_a(t,t)\,\mathrm dt=\frac{\coth a}{2a}-\frac1{2a^2}.
\textnormal{Differentiate the defining operator equation in a. The same zero-boundary Green inverse gives }\partial_aG_a(t,s)=-2a\int_0^1G_a(t,r)G_a(r,s)\,\mathrm dr.
\textnormal{Set }s=t\textnormal{, integrate, and use symmetry: the requested squared norm is }-\frac{T\prime(a)}{2a}\textnormal{ evaluated at }10.

solutionSteps: \operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t
q(t)=\frac{y\prime\prime(t)}{y\prime(t)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q\prime-\frac12q^2=-200,\quad q(0)=0
\textnormal{The positive first derivative permits a logarithm. Integrate its logarithmic derivative and use the initial slope.}
(\ln y\prime)\prime=q,\qquad y\prime(t)=10\operatorname{sech}^2(10t)
y(t)=\tanh(10t),\qquad y(1)=\tanh{\left(10 \right)}
